title: Empowered Product Teams (Marty Cagan, SVPG)
text:
Marty Cagan defines empowered product teams as ordinary people equipped to solve hard problems in ways customers love, yet that work for the business. As Cagan puts it, great teams are comprised of ordinary people that are empowered and inspired.

## Purpose: serve customers, not the business

The fundamental difference between strong and weak product organizations lies in purpose. In traditional companies, technology teams exist to serve the business. In strong product organizations, teams exist to serve the customers, in ways that meet the needs of the business. This distinction shapes team motivation, morale, and innovation capacity.

## Outcomes vs output, problems vs features

A critical accountability shift differentiates empowered teams. Feature teams are held responsible for shipping features, which is output. Empowered teams are accountable for delivering business results and customer value, which are outcomes. Empowered teams receive problem statements rather than feature specifications, and they determine the implementation approach independently while remaining answerable for measurable success.

## Three litmus tests for true empowerment

Cagan offers a self-assessment. First, staffing includes competent people of character across the necessary disciplines. Second, teams are given problems to solve, not feature lists. Third, teams answer to outcomes rather than output metrics. Leadership is responsible for product vision, strategy, principles, priorities, and ongoing evangelism, creating teams of missionaries, not mercenaries. Management is responsible for staffing, coaching, and assigning clear quarterly objectives.

title: The Product Operating Model: An Introduction (Marty Cagan, SVPG)
text:
Marty Cagan describes the product operating model as a conceptual model based on a set of first principles that distinguish how the strongest product companies work. It rests on three dimensions.

## How products are built

Small, frequent, and reliable releases, usually at a minimum of once every 2 weeks, but ideally continuously through CI/CD. This is about far more than engineering: it changes how the company de-risks and delivers value.

## How problems are solved

Teams are assigned problems to solve and desired outcomes to achieve, instead of being given a list of features to build. Any proposed solution must be valuable, usable, feasible, and viable. Product discovery is the work of figuring out solutions that satisfy all four risks: value risk (will customers buy or use it), usability risk (can users figure out how to use it), feasibility risk (can engineers build it), and business viability risk (does it work for the business).

## How you decide which problems to solve

Product leaders create a compelling customer-centric product vision and an insight-driven product strategy to identify the most critical problems that need to be solved. The model emphasizes principles over process as central to product culture, contrasting with traditional approaches that prioritize procedural compliance. This is a shift from projects and dates toward products and outcomes.

title: Continuous Discovery, definition (Teresa Torres, Product Talk)
text:
Teresa Torres defines continuous discovery as weekly touch points with customers by the team building the product, where they conduct small research activities in pursuit of a desired outcome.

## The key components

The cadence is weekly touchpoints, occurring every single week. The research is conducted by the team building the product, meaning the product manager, designer, and a software engineer engage with customers directly rather than relying on someone else's research. The activities are small research activities, including talking to customers, testing prototypes, and running experiments.

## Why weekly matters

The frequency requirement is what makes discovery continuous rather than a phase. The goal is to have multiple recent data points available whenever a product decision needs to be made, so teams stay continuously connected to customer reality and avoid the drift that happens when insights become stale or assumptions go unchallenged for too long. Torres pairs this habit with the opportunity solution tree, a visual that connects a desired business outcome to the customer opportunities and candidate solutions the team is exploring.

title: Jobs to Be Done Theory (Clayton Christensen Institute)
text:
The Christensen Institute defines Jobs to Be Done as a lens that reveals the circumstances, or forces, that drive people and organizations toward and away from decisions. Rather than relying on demographics or product features, the theory explores why people make choices by examining the functional, social, and emotional dimensions underlying their decisions.

## Hiring and firing products

People hire products or services when jobs arise in their lives, meaning they pull them into their lives to make progress. The institute stresses that conventional marketing's focus on market demographics or product attributes misses deeper motivations: people don't simply buy or pick products or services; they pull them into their lives to make progress.

## The milkshake study

A fast-food chain discovered that customers hired milkshakes for distinct jobs depending on circumstance. Morning customers sought hunger satiation and an engaging activity for a boring commute, and something they could hold easily in the car. Afternoon patrons wanted a treat for their children. Significantly, the competition wasn't other fast-food milkshakes, but rather bananas and bagels for the morning job, and other kids' treats for the afternoon job. Demographic or product-based analysis would have missed this entirely, which is why improving the milkshake based on a demographic profile of the average customer produced negligible impact on sales.

title: What Makes a Good vs Bad North Star Metric (Amplitude)
text:
A North Star Metric represents the single measure that best captures the core value your product delivers to customers. Amplitude contrasts good and bad choices.

## What makes a bad North Star metric

Bad North Star metrics tend to be vanity metrics that look good superficially but don't translate to meaningful business outcomes, or lagging indicators that reflect what already happened rather than predicting future results. An over-focus on revenue is a trap because revenue is a lagging indicator where what's done is done. Examples of poor choices: annual recurring revenue (ARR), monthly recurring revenue (MRR), daily active users (DAU), ad impressions, number of downloads, page views, registered users, story points delivered, and time on page.

## What makes a good North Star metric

A good North Star metric focuses on customer value, reflects the company vision so a reader understands the product strategy, is actionable and measurable so teams can influence it through their work, and is a leading indicator of revenue that predicts future business outcomes.

## Examples of good North Star metrics

Airbnb: nights booked. Spotify: time spent listening. Meta: active users. Amazon: purchases per month. Slack: teams reaching a threshold of messages sent. Uber: rides per week. Amplitude's own: weekly active users who had at least one question answered. The selection method: start from the customer's value moment, express it as specific measurable behavior, make it time-bound and within your control, confirm it is a leading indicator, and validate that it predicts retention and revenue in your data.

title: The Pmarca Guide to Startups, part 4: The only thing that matters (Marc Andreessen)
text:
Marc Andreessen popularized product/market fit in this 2007 essay. He defines it plainly: product/market fit means being in a good market with a product that can satisfy that market.

## The market wins (Rachleff's corollary)

Andreessen credits Andy Rachleff with the framing. When a great team meets a lousy market, market wins. When a lousy team meets a great market, market wins. When a great team meets a great market, something special happens. The number one company-killer is lack of market. In a great market, the market pulls product out of the startup: the product only needs to be viable, and customers actively seek it out. In a terrible market, you can have the best product in the world and an absolutely killer team, and it doesn't matter, you're going to fail.

## How you can feel it

You can always feel when product/market fit isn't happening. The customers aren't quite getting value out of the product, word of mouth isn't spreading, usage isn't growing that fast, press reviews are kind of blah, the sales cycle takes too long, and lots of deals never close. And you can always feel product/market fit when it's happening. The customers are buying the product just as fast as you can make it, or usage is growing just as fast as you can add more servers, and money from customers is piling up in your company checking account. Andreessen's advice: do whatever is required to get to product/market fit, including changing out people, rewriting the product, moving into a different market.

title: Sean Ellis Score / Sean Ellis Test for Product-Market Fit (Learning Loop)
text:
The Sean Ellis Test is a survey-based method for measuring product-market fit, developed by growth expert Sean Ellis.

## The core question and options

The survey asks users a single question: How would you feel if you could no longer use [product]? The three answer options are: very disappointed, somewhat disappointed, and not disappointed. The Sean Ellis Score is calculated as the number of respondents answering very disappointed divided by total respondents, times 100.

## The 40% threshold

A score of 40% or higher, meaning at least 40% of respondents select very disappointed, indicates that a product has likely achieved product-market fit. Ellis chose to ask about disappointment rather than satisfaction, because asking whether people like a product invites polite, positive answers, while asking how they would feel if it vanished reveals how necessary it is.

## Segmenting the very disappointed

Follow-up questions help identify the patterns behind the score: What is the main benefit you receive from the product? What type of person would most benefit from it? How can we improve it for you? These responses reveal which user segments find the product most essential and which value propositions resonate strongest, so a team below the threshold can double down on the users who are already highly disappointed at the thought of losing it.

title: What Is an MVP? Eric Ries Explains (Lean Startup Co.)
text:
Eric Ries defines the minimum viable product as that version of a new product which allows a team to collect the maximum amount of validated learning about customers with the least effort.

## MVP is not the smallest product

Ries emphasizes that MVP, despite the name, is not about creating minimal products. The purpose is learning, not minimalism. Pursuing an MVP requires intentional effort to extract learning from early iterations, which often involves substantial customer conversations and data analysis. The MVP is simply the fastest way to get through the Build-Measure-Learn feedback loop with the minimum amount of effort.

## Validated learning

The core principle is validated learning: building a sustainable business by learning through continuous experimentation and feedback from real customers, rather than by executing a detailed upfront plan. The goal of validated learning is to reduce uncertainty and risk by testing assumptions against real customer behavior, allowing teams to decide whether to persevere with the current strategy or pivot. If customers are satisfied with a minimum version, further development may not be necessary; if dissatisfaction emerges, another iteration is warranted.

title: The Kano Model (Noriaki Kano, via Wikipedia)
text:
The Kano model is a theory for product development and customer satisfaction developed by Professor Noriaki Kano in the 1980s, with his seminal paper published in April 1984. It classifies product attributes by their effect on customer satisfaction into five categories.

## The five categories

Must-be quality, also called basic: requirements that customers expect and take for granted. Good execution keeps customers neutral, but poor execution causes significant dissatisfaction. Example: functioning brakes in a car.

One-dimensional quality, also called performance: attributes that result in satisfaction when fulfilled and dissatisfaction when not fulfilled. These are the explicitly discussed features where companies compete. Example: fuel economy or acceleration.

Attractive quality, also called delighter or excitement: features that provide satisfaction when achieved fully, but do not cause dissatisfaction when not fulfilled. These unexpected features delight customers and differentiate a product.

Indifferent quality: aspects that are neither good nor bad and generate neither satisfaction nor dissatisfaction.

Reverse quality: a high degree of achievement that actually produces dissatisfaction, because preferences vary and some customers prefer a simpler product.

## Attributes decay over time

A critical dynamic: as competing products improve, attributes shift through the lifecycle. A once-delightful attribute gradually becomes an expected performance feature and then a basic must-be requirement as competitors catch up. This is why continual innovation is required: today's delighter is tomorrow's baseline expectation.

title: 12 Signs You're Working in a Feature Factory (John Cutler)
text:
John Cutler's widely cited list names the symptoms of an organization that ships features without regard for outcomes. It is the canonical anti-pattern description for product teams.

## The 12 signs

1. No measurement. Teams do not measure the impact of their work, or measurement is done in isolation by product management and selectively shared.
2. Rapid shuffling of teams and projects, aka Team Tetris. Instead of compelling missions, teams deal in feature and project assignments.
3. Success theater around shipping, with little discussion about impact. You can tell a great deal about an organization by what it celebrates.
4. Infrequent, acknowledged failures and scrapped work. Success is measured by features shipped rather than outcomes achieved, with little willingness to discard ineffective work.
5. No connection to core metrics. Teams cannot link their work to key business or customer objectives.
6. No PM retrospectives. Product managers lack a process to compare expected versus actual benefits of their decisions.
7. Obsessing about prioritization. Excessive effort to decide what to build, but minimal validation of whether the decision was correct.
8. No tweaking. Teams move immediately to the next project after shipping, without iterating based on feedback and performance data.
9. A culture of handoffs. Teams don't participate in research, validation, or post-launch support.
10. Large batches. Features delivered in single large releases rather than incrementally, despite using sprints.
11. Chasing upfront revenue. Features built primarily to close individual sales deals with weak economics and underestimated long-term complexity.
12. Shiny objects. Refactoring and technical debt work lack visibility, because success is measured by new feature output rather than product health.

title: Escaping the Build Trap (Melissa Perri, via Mind the Product)
text:
Melissa Perri's build trap is the state in which companies get stuck defining and shipping software with no measures of success, too busy managing the backlog and focusing on getting features out the door. It is an endless cycle where teams prioritize output volume over actual value creation, and it is closely related to the feature factory.

## The value exchange

Perri frames product work around a value exchange. Businesses create products or services to solve the problems, needs, or wants of customers. The customers only realize the value when their problems are solved. Then they give value back to companies in return, in the form of money or data. The build trap emerges when organizations associate value with the number of things they produce, features shipped, rather than the outcomes those features create. Value is not created by simply shipping features or copying competitors, but by figuring out what makes you valuable and sets you apart.

## Escaping the trap

Perri identifies three controllable internal factors for escaping: process, strategy, and culture. To escape, an organization must become customer-centric and reward learning and reaching outcomes, rather than focusing on output. The product manager's role in this model is to figure out what to build by connecting business goals to customer needs, not to administer a backlog or gather and prioritize stakeholder feature requests.

title: Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) (TechTarget)
text:
Business Process Model and Notation (BPMN) is an open standard to diagram a business process. It employs standardized graphics to represent participants, choices, and workflow, and is designed to be detailed yet comprehensible without specialized training.

## Maintenance and version

The Object Management Group (OMG) has overseen BPMN since 2005. BPMN 2.0 launched in 2011 and was updated to version 2.0.2 in 2014. The primary goal is to provide a standard notation readily understandable by all business users, from the executives and analysts who design processes to the technical staff who implement them.

## The four element categories

Flow objects comprise three types. Events are represented by circles and indicate something that happens during a process (start, intermediate, or end events). Activities are rounded rectangles and represent work done in a process. Gateways are diamonds and represent branching or merging points with decision logic.

Connecting objects link flow elements: sequence flows are solid lines showing order, message flows are dashed lines showing communication between participants, and associations are dotted lines linking artifacts to elements.

Swimlanes organize responsibilities through pools, which represent separate entities or participants, and lanes, which are internal divisions within a pool.

Artifacts provide clarifying information such as data objects, groups, and text annotations. BPMN aims to bridge communication gaps across departments using a universally interpretable visual language that transcends any specific implementation platform.

title: Alistair Cockburn's Use Cases, a guide (binaryphile, summarizing Writing Effective Use Cases)
text:
Alistair Cockburn's use case model captures what a system does in response to an actor's goal, independent of user interface design. A use case is a structured narrative of the interactions between actors and the system in pursuit of a goal.

## Primary actor, goal, and scope

The primary actor is the role that initiates the use case, and the goal is what that actor wants to achieve. Design scope defines the system under design, the black box whose boundary separates what is inside from what is external.

## Goal levels (the altitude metaphor)

Cockburn distinguishes three tiers. Summary level covers goals that encompass multiple user goals, measured in hours to years. User goal is the sea-level goal: it passes the boss test, meaning a supervisor would accept it as a meaningful piece of work, and it is typically completed in 3 to 9 steps in a single sitting. Subfunction is a supporting goal that is not independently valuable, measured in seconds.

## Main success scenario and extensions

The main success scenario (MSS) presents the happy path in roughly 3 to 9 steps, where each step is an interaction, a validation, or a state change. Extensions branch from specific MSS steps, keyed like 3a, 3b, or *a, and each extension concludes via rejoining the main flow, a separate success, or a failure.

## Stakeholders, interests, and guarantees

Identifying who cares and what they want prevents missing requirements. The template includes a minimal guarantee (what the system promises even on failure) and a success guarantee (the conditions true upon successful completion). The fully dressed format lists scope, level, primary and secondary actors, trigger, preconditions, stakeholders and interests, MSS, extensions, and both guarantees, contrasting with the casual format, which is a narrative paragraph only.

title: MoSCoW Prioritisation (Agile Business Consortium, DSDM)
text:
MoSCoW is a prioritisation technique from the DSDM agile framework, maintained by the Agile Business Consortium. The letters stand for Must Have, Should Have, Could Have, and Won't Have this time (the o's make the word pronounceable).

## The four categories

Must Have requirements are the Minimum Usable SubseT (MUST) that the project guarantees to deliver. They are non-negotiable: if not delivered, there is no viable reason to deploy the solution. A useful test is to ask whether cancelling the project would be the only sensible option if this requirement were not met.

Should Have requirements are important but not vital. They may be painful to leave out, but the solution is still viable without them, and a workaround may exist even if temporary or inefficient.

Could Have requirements are wanted or desirable but less important, with a smaller impact if left out. They form the primary pool of contingency.

Won't Have this time requirements are those the team has agreed will not be delivered in the current timeframe. Recording them clarifies scope and manages expectations.

## Effort distribution

DSDM recommends no more than 60% Must Have effort on a project; anything higher poses a risk to success and predictability unless the environment, technology, and team are all well understood and external risks are minimal. A sensible pool of Could Haves, typically around 20% of effort, provides the contingency that protects the timebox and on-time delivery. This directly counters the common anti-pattern of every requirement being labeled a Must Have, which removes all flexibility.

title: INVEST in Good Stories, and SMART Tasks (Bill Wake, XP123)
text:
Bill Wake coined the INVEST acronym in 2003 to describe the characteristics of a good user story, plus SMART for the tasks a story decomposes into.

## INVEST for stories

Independent: stories should not overlap in concept, and we'd like to be able to schedule and implement them in any order. Negotiable: a story is not an explicit contract for features; rather, details will be co-created by the customer and programmer during development. Valuable: a story needs to be valuable to the customer, so stories should be split vertically through the layers rather than by a single technical component, so each still delivers customer value. Estimable: a good story can be estimated with just enough precision to help the customer rank and schedule it. Small: good stories tend to be small, typically representing at most a few person-weeks of work. Testable: a good story is testable; writing a story card carries an implicit promise that I understand what I want well enough that I could write a test for it.

## SMART for tasks

Specific: a task needs to be specific enough that everyone can understand what's involved. Measurable: the key measure is, can we mark it as done, where done includes testing and refactoring. Achievable: the task owner should expect to be able to achieve the task. Relevant: every task should be relevant, contributing to the story at hand. Time-boxed: a task should be limited to a specific duration, so it does not expand indefinitely.

title: Writing Good Requirements (Karl Wiegers)
text:
Karl Wiegers, a leading authority on software requirements, defines the qualities of individual requirement statements and of the specification as a whole.

## Characteristics of quality requirement statements

Correct: each requirement must accurately describe the functionality to be delivered, checked against its source such as an actual customer. Feasible: you must be able to implement each requirement within the known capabilities and limitations of the system and its environment; involve developers early. Necessary: each requirement should document something the customers genuinely need or that conforms to an external requirement; trace it back to its origin to eliminate unnecessary gold-plating. Prioritized: assign an implementation priority (High: must incorporate, Medium: necessary but deferrable, Low: nice-to-have), because declaring everything equally critical removes the ability to respond to change. Unambiguous: the reader of a requirement should draw only one interpretation, and multiple readers should arrive at the same one. Verifiable: you must be able to devise tests or other checks to confirm the product properly implements the requirement; if you cannot verify it, compliance is a matter of opinion.

## Characteristics of the specification

Complete: the SRS should not be missing any requirements or necessary information; flag unknowns with TBD until resolved. Consistent: requirements must not conflict with each other or with higher-level requirements. Modifiable: you must be able to revise the SRS and maintain a change history, aided by unique labels and separately expressed requirements. Traceable: link each requirement to its source and forward to design elements, code, and test cases.

## Anti-pattern: ambiguous words to avoid

Wiegers warns against subjective terms that different readers interpret differently, including user-friendly, easy, simple, rapid, efficient, several, state-of-the-art, improved, maximize, and minimize. These words are the classic source of ambiguous, unverifiable requirements.

title: Gherkin Reference (Cucumber official documentation)
text:
Gherkin is a structured, plain-language format that uses a set of special keywords to give structure and meaning to executable specifications. Business analysts use it to write acceptance criteria that are unambiguous, testable, and readable by both stakeholders and developers.

## The keywords

Feature provides a high-level description of a software feature and groups related scenarios. Scenario (also written as Example) is a concrete example that illustrates a business rule, consisting of a list of steps. Given describes the initial context or preconditions, putting the system in a known state before the user starts interacting. When describes an event or action, typically the thing the person interacting with the system does. Then describes an expected outcome or result, verified with an observable assertion (not by checking internal database state). And and But connect successive steps of the same type to keep the specification readable. Background defines steps common to all scenarios in a feature, run before each one. Scenario Outline runs the same scenario multiple times with different data combinations supplied by an Examples table. Rule (added in Gherkin 6) groups together several scenarios that belong to a single business rule.

## Given-When-Then as acceptance criteria

The Given-When-Then structure gives a consistent framework for acceptance criteria that eliminates ambiguity: Given establishes context, When describes the trigger, and Then defines the expected response. Each step's text is matched to a code block called a step definition, which makes the specification executable. Together the steps form an executable specification of the system, so the acceptance criteria and the automated tests are the same living artifact.

title: User Stories and the Three C's (Mike Cohn, Mountain Goat Software)
text:
Mike Cohn defines a user story as a short, simple description of a feature told from the perspective of the person who desires the new capability, usually a user or customer of the system.

## The template

Stories typically follow the format: As a (type of user), I want (some goal) so that (some reason). The reason clause is what keeps the story anchored to user value rather than to a solution.

## The three C's (Ron Jeffries)

Cohn adopts Ron Jeffries's three C's to describe the working parts of a story. Card: a written description of the story used for planning and as a reminder; it is intentionally short because the story is meant to start a conversation, not finish one. Conversation: the discussions about the story that flesh out the details; every user story is a placeholder for a future conversation. Confirmation: the acceptance tests that convey and document details and determine when the story is complete.

## Not upfront specifications

The foundational principle is that user stories function as conversation prompts rather than complete written specifications. The written text is an incomplete requirement until the team and stakeholders discuss it, which shifts the focus from writing about features to discussing them and keeps the requirement flexible as understanding evolves. Good stories follow the INVEST characteristics (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable). This contrasts with use cases, which capture a more complete, structured interaction narrative for a goal.

title: Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM) (Perforce)
text:
A requirements traceability matrix (RTM) is a tool or document that maps the relationship between requirements and other artifacts like tests, issues, and source code. It ensures that every requirement can be followed through the lifecycle so nothing is overlooked.

## Why it matters

RTMs provide documented proof of compliance with standards such as DO-178C (aerospace), ISO 26262 (automotive), and FDA regulations (medical devices), which is essential in safety-critical industries. By linking each requirement to specific test cases, organizations guarantee comprehensive test coverage and validate that all specified needs are addressed.

## Types of traceability

Bidirectional traceability is the ability to trace forward (for example, from requirement to test case to defect) and backward (for example, from defect to test result to requirement). Forward tracing follows requirements through to test cases and defects to confirm each requirement is covered. Backward tracing connects defects and test cases back to originating requirements to confirm nothing extra was built (no scope creep or orphaned work).

## What RTMs link and their benefits

Requirements connect to test cases, design specifications, source code, issues and defects, and risk assessments. Key benefits: demonstrating regulatory compliance with auditable documentation, ensuring complete test coverage, enabling rapid impact analysis when requirements change, providing real-time project visibility across stakeholders, and identifying gaps and high-risk areas early for proactive risk mitigation.

title: ISO/IEC 25010 Product Quality Model (Perforce)
text:
ISO/IEC 25010 is the international standard that defines a product quality model, and it is the canonical taxonomy business analysts use to structure non-functional requirements (also called quality attributes or quality of service requirements). It organizes product quality into eight characteristics, each with sub-characteristics.

## The eight quality characteristics

Functional Suitability: how well the product provides functions meeting stated and implied needs. Sub-characteristics: functional completeness, functional correctness, functional appropriateness.

Performance Efficiency: performance relative to the amount of resources used. Sub-characteristics: time behavior, resource utilization, capacity.

Compatibility: how well a product can exchange information with other products and co-exist in a shared environment. Sub-characteristics: co-existence, interoperability.

Usability: how well the product can be used to achieve goals effectively, efficiently, and with satisfaction. Sub-characteristics: appropriateness recognizability, learnability, operability, user error protection, user interface aesthetics, accessibility.

Reliability: how well the system performs specified functions under specified conditions. Sub-characteristics: maturity, availability, fault tolerance, recoverability.

Security: how well the product protects information and data. Sub-characteristics: confidentiality, integrity, non-repudiation, accountability, authenticity.

Maintainability: how well the product can be modified to correct, improve, or adapt it. Sub-characteristics: modularity, reusability, analysability, modifiability, testability.

Portability: how well the product can be transferred from one environment to another. Sub-characteristics: adaptability, installability, replaceability.

Capturing NFRs against this model, with measurable targets (for example a 95th-percentile response time, or an availability percentage), prevents the common anti-pattern of specifying only functional behavior and discovering quality gaps late.

title: The BABOK Elicitation Knowledge Area and its Tasks (Modern Analyst)
text:
The BABOK Elicitation knowledge area organizes the work of drawing out requirements from stakeholders into a structured set of tasks and techniques. Elicitation is deliberate: it is not merely collecting requirements that stakeholders hand over, but actively uncovering needs, including unstated ones.

## The key tasks

Prepare for Elicitation: the analyst identifies which techniques to use based on the business domain, environment, team skill level, stakeholder openness, and required deliverables. Conduct Elicitation Activity: the actual execution of the selected techniques to gather requirements from stakeholders. Document Elicitation Results: recording and organizing the information obtained. Confirm Elicitation Results: validating that the captured information accurately reflects stakeholder needs, which guards against misinterpretation.

## The elicitation techniques

BABOK identifies nine commonly used techniques: Brainstorming (rapid, uncritical generation of a broad set of options), Document Analysis (reviewing existing documentation), Focus Groups (facilitated group discussion), Interface Analysis (identifying interactions between systems or components), Interviews (structured or unstructured questioning of a person or group), Observation (studying stakeholders in their actual work environment, useful for current-process detail), Prototyping (surfacing user-interface and interaction requirements through a tangible model), Requirements Workshops (structured, facilitated sessions combining several techniques in small groups), and Survey or Questionnaire (gathering input from many stakeholders efficiently).

## Choosing techniques

Elicitation techniques can be combined in any way that achieves the best result, but elicitation is not about using as many techniques as possible; the analyst selects techniques that fit the situation, stakeholders, and the kind of information needed.
